facts.t: The longest Act the British Parliament had ever passed
facts.d: The Government of India Act, 1935 ran to 321 sections and 10 schedules. It was so bulky that it had to be split into two separate bills at Westminster — one of which became the Government of Burma Act, formally separating Burma from India.

facts.t: The Federal Court heard barely 135 cases in 13 years
facts.d: Set up in 1937 under the Act, it sat in the Chamber of Princes inside the Parliament building — the same room the Supreme Court of India would use until 1958. Its tiny caseload masked its importance: it was India's first federal umpire.

facts.t: The Act was rejected by everyone it was written for
facts.d: Nehru called it a machine with strong brakes and no engine; Jinnah called it thoroughly rotten and unacceptable. The All-India Federation it proposed never came into being — yet nearly 250 of its provisions were carried into the Constitution of India.

bank.q: With reference to the Government of India Act, 1935, consider the following statements:
s: It provided for an All-India Federation which came into existence after the provincial elections of 1937.
It abolished dyarchy in the provinces but introduced dyarchy at the Centre.
It expanded the electorate from about 3% to about 14% of the population.
bank.e: Statement 1 is wrong — the Federation was to come into being only after sufficient princely states acceded, which never happened. Statements 2 and 3 are correct: provincial dyarchy ended while dyarchy was introduced at the Centre, and the franchise widened from roughly 3% to 14%.

bank.q: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched as a legacy of the 1935 Act?
o: Federal Court — institutional predecessor of the Supreme Court of India
Three-fold division of legislative subjects — Union, State and Concurrent Lists
Separate electorates — origin of the common electoral roll
Federal and Provincial Public Service Commissions — framework behind Articles 315–323
bank.e: Separate electorates were abandoned, not inherited. The Constitution replaced communal electorates with a common electoral roll and provided affirmative representation through reservation of seats instead.

bank.as: The Government of India Act, 1935 is described as India's constitutional rehearsal without sovereignty.
bank.rs: Defence and external affairs remained under the direct control of the Governor-General, and Governors retained discretionary and emergency powers.
bank.e: Both are true and the Reason explains the Assertion precisely. Indians got the machinery of government — legislatures, ministries, a federal court — while the substance of sovereign power stayed with the Crown's representatives.

bank.q: The Reserve Bank of India began operations on:
bank.e: The RBI Act was passed in 1934; the Bank began operations on 1 April 1935, the same year as the Act — part of the same drive toward centralised modern financial governance.

bank.q: Match List I (feature of the 1935 Act) with List II (its constitutional descendant):
pairs: D. Governor-General's power to legislate between sessions
bank.e: Federal Court → Supreme Court; Federal PSC → Arts 315–323; Concurrent List → Seventh Schedule; the Governor-General's between-sessions legislative power → the ordinance power now in Arts 123 and 213.

bank.q: Which one of the following was NOT a feature of the Government of India Act, 1935?
o: Justiciable Fundamental Rights enforceable in courts
Emergency and reserve powers for Governors
bank.e: The 1935 Act contained no justiciable Fundamental Rights — that is precisely the break the Constitution made. Everything else listed was present in some form.

bank.q: Consider the following contrasts between the 1935 Act and the Constitution of 1950:
s: Sovereignty moved from the British Crown to the people of India.
The colonial framework was police-state oriented, while the Constitution is welfare-state oriented.
Both documents vested real discretionary power in Governors.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong — under the Constitution, Governors are generally constitutional heads, not repositories of real colonial discretion.

bank.q: Arrange the following in correct chronological order:
items: Reserve Bank of India Act passed
Provincial elections held under the new Act
Reserve Bank of India begins operations
bank.e: RBI Act 1934 → Government of India Act 1935 → RBI operations from 1 April 1935 → provincial elections 1937. Note the trap: the RBI Act precedes the 1935 Act, but RBI operations begin the same year as the Act.

bank.q: Under the 1935 Act, in the event of repugnancy between a federal law and a provincial law in the Concurrent field:
o: The Federal Court decided by majority
bank.e: Federal law prevailed on repugnancy in the concurrent field — the direct ancestor of Article 254 and one root of India's strong-Centre bias.

bank.q: The 1935 Act contributed all of the following to India's federal imagination EXCEPT:
o: A strong-Centre bias that was inherited and strengthened
Emergency centralisation as a normal constitutional device
The idea of federalism resting on democratic legitimacy
A federal court acting as constitutional umpire
bank.e: Federalism resting on democratic legitimacy is what the Constitution added by rejecting the Act's model. The framers' verdict was that federalism without democracy was not worth inheriting.

bank.q: The All-India Federation contemplated by the Act was to comprise:
o: British Indian provinces and acceding princely states
Only those princely states that signed the Instrument of Accession in 1947
Provinces, princely states and French and Portuguese possessions
bank.e: It was to federate British Indian provinces with princely states, but only once enough princely states acceded. They never did in sufficient numbers, so the federal part of the Act stayed on paper.

bank.q: Consider the following about representation under the 1935 Act:
s: Separate electorates were continued for Muslims, Sikhs and others.
Universal adult suffrage was introduced for provincial elections.
Communal representation was reflected in the composition of provincial legislatures.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong — the franchise was widened to about 14%, still far from universal adult suffrage, which arrived only with the Constitution.
